content: Preterm infants are born with insufficient skeletal stores of calcium and phosphorus. Human milk from preterm mothers does not provide adequate amounts of these minerals to meet the nutritional needs of preterm infants for optimal growth. Supplementing human milk with calcium and phosphorus has been proposed as a strategy to enhance the growth and development of these infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether adding calcium and phosphorus supplements to human milk improves growth and bone metabolism in preterm infants without causing significant adverse effects. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies up to April 2016. Clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared supplementation of human milk with calcium and/or phosphorus versus no supplementation in hospitalized preterm infants. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the included trials using Cochrane methods. Dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RRs), and continuous outcomes were reported as mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. This review is an update of a 2001 review, which found no eligible trials. In this updated review, only one trial involving 40 preterm infants met the inclusion criteria. The quality of evidence from this trial was judged to be low due to methodological concerns, including inadequate reporting of randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding, as well as imprecision due to the small sample size and wide confidence intervals. The trial found no significant differences in neonatal growth outcomes, such as weight, length, or head circumference, between the supplementation group and the non-supplementation group at any of the reported time points (two, four, or six weeks postnatal age). At six weeks postnatal age, infants who received calcium and phosphorus supplementation had a reduction in serum alkaline phosphatase concentration (MD -56.85 IU/L, 95% CI -101.27 to -12.43). However, this finding is unlikely to have clinical significance. The trial did not provide data on other important outcomes, such as growth at 12 to 18 months, neonatal fractures, feed intolerance, breastfeeding, or long-term childhood outcomes like fractures, growth, or neurodevelopmental measures. In conclusion, this review identified only one small trial with low-quality evidence comparing calcium and phosphorus supplementation of human milk versus no supplementation in hospitalized preterm infants. The evidence did not demonstrate any clinically significant differences in growth or other important outcomes. Although a reduction in serum alkaline phosphatase concentration was observed in the supplementation group, this finding is not considered clinically meaningful. Given the advent of multi-component human milk fortifiers, which include a broader range of nutrients, supplementation of human milk with calcium and/or phosphorus alone is no longer a common practice. Therefore, further trials of this specific intervention are unlikely to be beneficial. Future research should focus on evaluating the effects of multi-component fortifiers with varying mineral compositions on clinically important outcomes during the neonatal period and later in childhood.
